newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PM SAYS COMPROMISE ON NATIVE TITLE PLAN NOT POSSIBLE
The Prime Minister says while he has agreed to discuss his 10-point native title plan with Labor, there will not be any compromise on the basic principles.
Mr Howard will meet Opposition Leader Kim Beazley in a bid to find common ground on the Government's response to the High Court's Wik decision.
He says legislation to give effect to the plan will be drafted by mid-June.
Mr Howard says he is ready to discuss detail at the margin, but it would be misleading of him to suggest significant compromise is possible.
PM SAYS FUEL REBATE PROPOSALS FAIR AND REASONABLE
The Prime Minister says he has no doubt the mining industry will realise that the Government's decision to cap the diesel fuel rebate is fair and reasonable.
The Government has told the mining industry it wants to cut rebate payments from 823-million dollars last year to 813 this year.
The Minerals Council says the decision will drastically increase the cost of fuel for mining companies and make Australia uncompetitive.
But John Howard says the Government's proposals are fair.
JUDGE WARNS OF COURTS BEING USED TO SUPPRESS DEBATE

A dismissing a scientist's attempt to sue a church elder over claims surrounding Noah's Ark, a Federal Court judge has warned about the dangers of the legal system interferring in religious and ideological debate.
In a case which pitted creationist against scientist, Melbourne University's Professor Ian Plimer today lost his legal action against Christian Minister Doctor Alan Roberts.
The professor alleged Doctor Roberts had made false claims about his involvement in the dig for Noah's Ark in Turkey.

In handing down his judgement, Justice Ronald Sackville warned that in matters such as religion and ideology, caution must be exercised to avoid the courts being used to suppress debate and discussion on issues of general interest.
COMMITTEE SAYS APOLOGY WILL NOT LEAD TO MILLIONS IN PAYOUTS
The Deaths in Custody Watch Committee in Perth says an apology to the "Stolen Generation" by Federal parliament, will not necessarily lead to millions of dollars in payouts.
The committee also says any form of apology in the Parliament would not be seen as legally binding upon the Commenwealth.
The committee's Glenn Shaw says theoretically state governments would be liable for compensation claims because it was State legislation that removed Aboriginal children from their families.
But Mr Shaw says many Aboriginal people do not want money, and recommendations such as access to counselling and family support should be implemented.
CENTRE WELCOMES MOVE TOWARDS UNIFORMITY ON DRUG LAWS
The head of the National Centre for Education and Training on Addiction says unless something is done to address the demand for drugs, there will always be people willing to supply.

Steve Allsop has welcomed moves to toughen Australia's drug laws. A discussion paper by the Standing Committee of Attorneys General, which has recommended stricter penalties, and moves towards greater uniformity around the nation.
Mr Allsop says there is a need for flexible uniform laws.
But he says, while tougher penalties will help combat the drug trade, it is just one part of the strategy to reduce drug trafficking.
KNIGHT UNHAPPY WITH HOTELS OVER OLYMPIC BEDS
In New South Wales, Olympics Minister Michael Knight, says if a lack of cooperation by some hotels regarding the planned bed tax continues, it will be an active act of sabotage' of the Olympics.
At an estimates committe hearing in Parliament this afternoon, Mr Knight made clear his unhappiness with the hotel industry even before the 10 per cent tax was proposed.
He says that tax 'added salt to the wound' for hoteliers who had delayed signing contracts guaranteeing hotel space.
Mr Knight says he's informed the estimates committee that out of the 25,000 beds required, only 8,000 have been contracted.
FIRST AUSTRALIAN WOMAN TO CLIMB EVEREST TO RECEIVE STATE RECEPTION
The first Australian woman to climb Mount Everest says she'll accept the Victorian Premier's offer of a state reception in her honour.
Thirty-nine-year-old Brigitte Muir, from the Wimmera town of Natimuk, has arrived home after spending more than a month in freezing conditions.
Ms Muir, who conquered the world's highest mountain on her fourth attempt, says standing on the summit was awe inspiring.
Ms Muir says she is happy to accept Premier Jeff Kennett's offer of a reception but her next big challenge is to spend a couple of days lying on a beach.
